headline: Light Speed: AYZ and the Co-Packaged Optics Bet That Made Readers Reach for Their Brokerage Apps
lede: A Substack analyst known only as AYZ published a February 2026 deep-dive on co-packaged optics — the technology NVIDIA is deploying to rewire the nervous system of its AI data centres — and the response was a familiar one: readers read the disclaimer, then immediately invested anyway.
body:
AYZ publishes "Global Technology Research" on Substack and goes by @ayz_yzyz on X, writing with the density of a sell-side initiating report but without a bulge-bracket bank's compliance team in tow. The newsletter covers semiconductor and technology themes across Asia and the United States, attracting retail investors hunting for pre-consensus ideas in the supply chains that power artificial intelligence. Its February 2026 piece on co-packaged optics exemplifies the appeal: technically detailed, laced with stock-specific implications, and fronted by the obligatory disclaimer that none of it constitutes financial advice. That disclaimer, as jukan05 noted with some amusement, was not exactly a cold shower.

The thesis concerns a fundamental shift in how AI data centres move information between chips. Traditional networking hardware uses pluggable transceivers — discrete, hot-swappable modules that bolt onto the edge of a switch and convert electrical signals into light for fibre transmission. Co-packaged optics (CPO) discards the plug: the laser engine moves directly inside the switch's silicon package, inches from the processor rather than at the end of a long, lossy electrical trace. NVIDIA's own figures put signal loss in a conventional 200 Gb/s channel at up to 22 dB; CPO cuts it to roughly 4 dB. Power consumption per interface falls from approximately 30 watts to as low as 9 watts — savings that compound dramatically across an AI factory running thousands of networked GPUs.

NVIDIA's CPO portfolio runs on two tracks. Quantum-X Photonics, the InfiniBand switching product, offers 144 ports at 800 Gb/s apiece (115 Tb/s total) and became available in early 2026. Spectrum-X Photonics, the Ethernet counterpart, follows in the second half of 2026, ranging from 102.4 Tb/s to 409.6 Tb/s. The broader validation came from Broadcom, whose Tomahawk 6 Davisson — the industry's first 102.4-Tbps merchant-silicon Ethernet switch with fully integrated CPO — began shipping in late 2025. Where Broadcom ships, the rest of the data-centre industry eventually follows.

For AYZ's readers, the trade was never about NVDA itself — already priced for dominance. The alpha sits in the supply chain. In March 2026, NVIDIA formalised that chain with a $4 billion combined investment in Lumentum Holdings (LITE) and Coherent Corp (COHR), split equally, covering purchase commitments and access rights to laser components: Lumentum makes CPO-optimised emitters at 1,311 nanometres; Coherent supplies comparable modules. Further down, InnoLight (now TeraHop) and Eoptolink hold roughly 60% of NVIDIA's 800G pluggable module orders, while TFC Optical Communications (300394.SZ), a Shenzhen-listed fibre-optics maker supplying NVIDIA's 1.6-terabit silicon photonics engine, was trading at over 130 times forward earnings by early 2026 — a multiple that blends genuine strategic value with the speculative premium attached to any supplier NVIDIA endorses.

The meta-observation in jukan05's tweet describes something real about how financial information circulates on Substack. The disclaimer — "this is not financial advice" — has become infrastructure rather than guardrail. AYZ's credibility rests on a track record: an earlier note on the Japanese polishing-materials maker Mipox preceded a doubling of the stock within two weeks. That kind of hit rate, amplified through X reposts, turns a newsletter into something closer to a conviction trade alert, regardless of the header. The dynamic is not unique to AYZ: long-form, research-flavoured Substack publishing provides just enough apparent rigour to move capital at scale, while the disclaimer protects only the author. Regulators have been slow to close the gap, partly because the line between diligent retail commentary and unlicensed advice is genuinely blurry, and partly because the platforms have no incentive to draw it.

concepts.definition: A networking technology that integrates the laser-based optical engine directly into the silicon package of a switch or processor, replacing the separate pluggable transceiver modules used in conventional data-centre networking. By shortening the electrical path between chip and light source, CPO cuts signal loss, reduces power consumption per port by two-thirds or more, and removes a class of discrete failure points — at the cost of losing the field-replaceability that pluggable transceivers provide.

A hot-swappable module — typically in QSFP, OSFP, or similar form factors — that clips onto the faceplate of a network switch and converts electrical data signals into optical pulses for fibre transmission. The dominant interconnect standard in data centres for the past two decades, but increasingly constrained by the long electrical trace lengths and consequent signal loss as per-port bandwidth approaches 800 Gb/s and beyond.

The boilerplate notice — 'this is not financial advice,' 'for informational purposes only,' or equivalent — that independent investment commentators prepend to their analysis. In legal terms it is intended to distinguish commentary from regulated investment advice, which requires licensing in most jurisdictions. In practice, on high-conviction Substack newsletters with demonstrable track records, the disclaimer functions as a formality that readers absorb and then disregard.

The engineering discipline of fabricating optical components — waveguides, modulators, photodetectors — using standard silicon manufacturing processes (chiefly CMOS). It enables the optical engines used in CPO to be manufactured at semiconductor scale and cost rather than as bespoke photonic components, which is the key enabler of volume CPO deployment.

The two competing networking protocols for connecting GPU clusters. InfiniBand, historically dominant in HPC and now championed by NVIDIA's Quantum-X product line, offers lower latency and tighter integration with NVIDIA's CUDA software stack. Ethernet, the universal standard for enterprise networking, is increasingly competitive for large-scale AI training — particularly through NVIDIA's Spectrum-X platform — and is preferred by hyperscalers seeking vendor diversity.

fact_check: Core technical claims check out against NVIDIA's own published specifications: Quantum-X Photonics at 115 Tb/s / 144 × 800 Gb/s ports, Spectrum-X SN6810 at 102.4 Tb/s, SN6800 at 409.6 Tb/s; CPO power reduction from ~30W to ~9W per interface; electrical loss reduction from ~22 dB to ~4 dB. The $4B NVIDIA investment in Lumentum and Coherent is confirmed by NVIDIA and SiliconANGLE (March 2026). Broadcom Tomahawk 6 Davisson (102.4 Tbps CPO) is a Broadcom product, not an NVIDIA product — relevant because AYZ's piece discusses the broader CPO landscape, not solely NVIDIA's own switches. Innolight / Eoptolink's 60% wallet-share figure on 800G modules is corroborated by trade-press reporting. TFC Optical's role as a silicon-photonics supplier with 2026 volume-production targets is cited in supply-chain analysis; at 138× forward earnings in early 2026 it carries substantial speculation premium. The 'Mipox doubling in two weeks' claim appears in secondary coverage of AYZ's track record and has not been independently verified against exchange data.
thread_summary: jukan05 reposts AYZ's February 2026 CPO/NVIDIA Substack with warm endorsement, noting the irony of reading a 'not financial advice' disclaimer and immediately investing — a reaction that both validates AYZ's analytical credibility and illustrates the thin line between newsletter commentary and market-moving recommendation.
